objectives: Explain regenerative agriculture practices — cover crops, no-till, crop rotation, and agroforestry — and their role in building soil organic carbon.
Quantify nitrogen and water footprints and connect them to planetary-boundary and food-security challenges to 2050.
Describe CRISPR gene editing, vertical farming, and climate-smart agriculture as frontier technologies in the food system.

slides.title: Regenerative agriculture — cover crops, no-till, rotation, and soil carbon
slides.body:
Conventional intensive agriculture — deep tillage, bare fallows, high synthetic inputs, monocultures — achieved extraordinary yield gains in the 20th century but at significant ecological cost: soil erosion, organic matter loss, nitrate leaching, and greenhouse gas emissions. **Sustainable agriculture** seeks to maintain productivity indefinitely without degrading the resource base. **Regenerative agriculture** goes further, aiming to actively rebuild soil health, biodiversity, and ecosystem services.

The core practices of regenerative systems are well established in the scientific literature:

**Cover crops** are non-cash crops grown between main-crop seasons primarily to protect and improve the soil. Leguminous cover crops — **hairy vetch (*Vicia villosa*)**, **crimson clover (*Trifolium incarnatum*)**, **winter peas (*Pisum sativum* subsp. *arvense*)** — fix atmospheric N$_2$ via *Rhizobium* symbiosis, contributing 50–200 kg N/ha that substitutes for synthetic fertiliser. Grasses — **cereal rye (*Secale cereale*)**, **oats (*Avena sativa*)** — add biomass, reduce erosion, and suppress weeds. Brassicas — **oilseed radish (*Raphanus sativus*)** — break compaction with deep taproots. The **Rodale Institute** (Kutztown, Pennsylvania) has conducted the longest-running side-by-side comparison of organic and conventional systems (the **Farming Systems Trial**, initiated 1981), documenting equivalent yields in organic systems after a transition period and significantly higher soil organic matter accumulation.

**No-till and conservation tillage** — leaving crop residues on the surface and disturbing soil minimally — reduce erosion, preserve soil structure, and sequester carbon by minimising the oxidative decomposition triggered by ploughing. The adoption of no-till in the US and South America (particularly in the Brazilian Cerrado) has been one of the most significant soil conservation achievements of the last 40 years. By 2020, approximately 12% of global cropland (around 200 million ha) was under some form of conservation tillage (FAO data). **Rolf Derpsch** (formerly IITA/FAO) is a leading researcher on global no-till adoption.

**Crop rotation** — sequencing different crop species across seasons on the same land — breaks pest and disease cycles, improves soil biology, reduces input requirements, and, when legumes are included, reduces fertiliser N demand. The **corn–soybean rotation** is the dominant rotation in the US Corn Belt; the **wheat–canola–pulse rotation** is standard in the Canadian Prairies. Long rotations of four or more crops (corn–soybean–wheat–red clover) substantially reduce herbicide use and build organic matter compared to continuous corn.

**Soil organic carbon (SOC)** — measured as a percentage of soil mass — is the central metric of soil health. Each 1% increase in SOC in the top 30 cm of a hectare of soil stores approximately 23–30 tonnes of carbon. The **4 per 1000 Initiative** (launched at COP21, Paris 2015, by French agricultural minister **Stéphane Le Foll**) proposed that increasing global SOC stocks by 0.4% per year would offset the entire annual increase in atmospheric CO$_2$ from fossil fuels. While the full offset claim is debated, the initiative crystallised international policy attention on soil carbon sequestration.

**Agroforestry** — integrating trees with crops or livestock — combines the ecological benefits of forests (carbon storage, water regulation, biodiversity) with agricultural productivity. **Alley cropping** (food crops grown between rows of trees), **silvopasture** (trees and pasture), and **multistrata agroforestry** (multi-layered tropical systems) are the main forms. **The World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF)**, based in Nairobi, documents that agroforestry systems can sequester 2–5 tonnes C/ha/year while maintaining food production — making them among the most cost-effective land-based climate mitigation options. The landmark **Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change** (2006, by **Nicholas Stern**) identified avoided deforestation and land-use change as the largest single available mitigation opportunity, providing the policy rationale that elevated agroforestry and reforestation in climate negotiations.

slides.title: Nitrogen and water footprints — planetary boundaries and the 2050 challenge
slides.body:
Food systems are the dominant driver of two of the nine **planetary boundaries** identified by **Johan Rockström** and colleagues in their 2009 *Nature* paper: **biogeochemical flows (nitrogen and phosphorus cycles)** and **freshwater use**. Both are already transgressed according to the 2023 update by **Katherine Richardson** and colleagues in *Science Advances*.

**The nitrogen footprint** of food:

The **Haber-Bosch process** (Fritz Haber, patent 1910; Carl Bosch, industrial scale at BASF, 1913) converts atmospheric N$_2$ to ammonia (NH$_3$) using natural gas as energy and hydrogen source. It now produces approximately 175 million tonnes of NH$_3$ per year, underpinning about half of the nitrogen in global food production. Without Haber-Bosch, Earth could support roughly 4 billion people at current diet composition — the process enabled the population growth of the 20th century. However, the nitrogen cycle is severely perturbed: reactive nitrogen (Nr) losses from agriculture include nitrate leaching to groundwater, ammonia volatilisation from manure and urea, and **nitrous oxide (N$_2$O)** emissions from denitrification. N$_2$O is a greenhouse gas with a 100-year global warming potential of **298 times CO$_2$** (IPCC AR6), and agriculture contributes approximately 10–12% of total global GHG emissions, with N$_2$O accounting for around a third of that.

The **nitrogen use efficiency (NUE)** of global cereal production averages only 30–50% — meaning more than half the applied N is lost to the environment. **4R Nutrient Stewardship** (right source, right rate, right time, right place) is the industry-standard framework promoted by the **International Plant Nutrition Institute (IPNI)** and its successor **IPNI's integration into the Fertilizer Canada / CropLife / IFA** frameworks for improving NUE.

**The water footprint** of food:

Agriculture accounts for approximately 70% of global freshwater withdrawals (FAO AQUASTAT). The **virtual water** concept — developed by **Tony Allan** (King's College London, 1993) — quantifies the water embedded in traded commodities: producing 1 kg of beef requires approximately 15,000 litres of water; 1 kg of wheat, ~1,500 litres; 1 kg of soybean, ~2,500 litres. **Water footprint accounting** (formalised by **Arjen Hoekstra** at the University of Twente, *The Water Footprint of Production and Consumption*, 2011) distinguishes green water (rain), blue water (irrigation from rivers/groundwater), and grey water (water needed to dilute pollutants).

**Groundwater depletion** in major aquifers — the **Ogallala Aquifer** (US Great Plains), the **Indo-Gangetic Plain aquifers** (India and Pakistan), and the **North China Plain aquifer** — is one of the most serious long-term food-security threats. GRACE satellite gravity measurements (NASA/DLR) have documented net depletion of 10–30 km$^3$/year in each of these systems.

**Climate-smart agriculture (CSA)**, championed by the **FAO** since the 2010 Hague Conference on Agriculture, Food Security and Climate Change, addresses the triple challenge of: (1) sustainably increasing productivity and incomes; (2) adapting to climate change; (3) reducing and removing GHG emissions. The **CGIAR Research Program on Climate Change, Agriculture and Food Security (CCAFS)**, led by the **Alliance of Bioversity International and CIAT**, produces the evidence base for CSA interventions across major farming systems.

**Food security to 2050**: The **FAO's 2009 World Summit on Food Security** widely cited a projection that feeding 9–10 billion people by 2050 would require increasing food production by 70%. This figure was challenged by **Tim Benton** and others as confounding production with demand; later analyses (notably **Foley et al. 2011** in *Nature* — "Solutions for a cultivated planet") showed that closing yield gaps on existing cropland, reducing food waste (one-third of all food calories are lost or wasted — **FAO 2011 SAVE FOOD initiative**), and shifting diets toward less animal protein could meet 2050 demand without major cropland expansion. The **EAT-Lancet Commission Report** (2019, led by **Walter Willett** of Harvard School of Public Health) quantified a "planetary health diet" compatible with both human health and planetary boundaries.

slides.title: CRISPR crops, vertical farming, and the frontiers of food production
slides.body:
The frontier of agricultural technology in the 2020s combines molecular biotechnology, controlled-environment agriculture, and digital intelligence to address the challenges identified in the planetary-boundary and food-security literature.

**CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing** was adapted for eukaryotic cells by **Jennifer Doudna** (UC Berkeley) and **Emmanuelle Charpentier** (then at Umeå University, Sweden; later Max Planck Unit for the Science of Pathogens, Berlin), whose 2012 paper in *Science* — "A Programmable Dual-RNA–Guided DNA Endonuclease in Adaptive Bacterial Immunity" — described the mechanism. They received the **2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry** for this work. Unlike transgenic GMO approaches that insert foreign DNA, CRISPR can make precise edits — insertions, deletions, or point mutations — at specific genomic loci, enabling trait changes indistinguishable from natural mutations.

Agricultural CRISPR applications in development or early commercialisation:

- **Waxy corn** (*Zea mays*): CRISPR knockout of the *Wx1* waxy gene producing high-amylopectin starch for food and industrial uses. Corteva commercialised **Waxy Corn** as the first CRISPR crop approved by USDA APHIS (2020) under the non-regulated pathway (since no foreign DNA is introduced).
- **High-oleic soybean**: **Calyxt** (now Cibus) used TALEN editing (a CRISPR precursor) to knock out *FAD2* genes producing a soybean oil with 80% oleic acid content, replacing partially hydrogenated oils. First commercial acreage in 2019.
- **Powdery mildew–resistant wheat**: **Rothamsted Research** and **CSIRO** groups edited *Mlo* genes in wheat, recapitulating resistance alleles from barley without introducing foreign DNA.
- **Late blight–resistant potato**: The **Wageningen University & Research** DuRPh project used cisgenesis (genes only from the same or compatible species) to stack *Phytophthora infestans* resistance genes, with CRISPR editing accelerating the work.
- **Drought-tolerant maize**: **Bayer CropScience / CSIRO** collaboration on editing **ARGOS8** gene regulation to modulate ethylene sensitivity under drought stress.

The regulatory landscape for CRISPR crops varies internationally: the US (USDA SECURE rule, 2020) largely does not regulate gene-edited crops that could have arisen through conventional breeding; the EU has proposed a new regulation (2023) to deregulate most precision breeding (CRISPR) products; China has approved gene-edited soybean and corn varieties; many countries have not yet established clear frameworks.

**Vertical farming** — growing crops in multi-layer controlled environments under LED lighting, often without soil (hydroponics, aeroponics) — addresses land scarcity, water efficiency, and supply chain resilience for high-value crops (leafy greens, herbs, strawberries). Companies including **AeroFarms** (Newark, New Jersey), **Bowery Farming** (New York), and **Plenty** (backed by SoftBank Vision Fund) have built commercial-scale indoor farms. Water use in vertical farms is 95–99% less than field production; pesticide use is near zero; year-round production is possible in any climate. The constraint is **energy**: LED lighting and HVAC systems consume 100–200 kWh per kg of leafy greens produced — making vertical farming economically viable only for high-value crops and dependent on low-carbon electricity to have a climate advantage over field production.

**The planetary boundaries** framework (**Johan Rockström et al., 2009**, *Nature*; updated by **Katherine Richardson et al., 2023**, *Science Advances*) identifies nine Earth-system processes with quantified boundaries: climate change, biodiversity loss, land-system change, freshwater change, biogeochemical flows, ocean acidification, stratospheric ozone, aerosol loading, and novel entities. Agriculture is the primary driver of transgression in four: biogeochemical flows (N, P), land-system change (deforestation), freshwater change (irrigation), and biodiversity loss. Addressing these simultaneously while feeding 9–10 billion people by 2050 is what **Gordon Conway** (author of *One Billion Hungry: Can We Feed the World?*, 2012) and others have called the "doubly green revolution" — more food, less environmental impact, equitably distributed.

question.question: A corn field produces a yield of 10 t/ha of grain. The nitrogen content of corn grain is approximately 1.5% N by dry weight. The total N applied as synthetic fertiliser was 220 kg N/ha. Assuming no other N inputs, calculate the nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) as a percentage, defined as: NUE (%) = (N removed in grain / N applied) × 100. Round to one decimal place.
question.hint: N in grain = 10,000 kg/ha × 0.015 = 150 kg N/ha. NUE = (150 / 220) × 100 = 68.2%. Note this simplified NUE ignores N from soil mineralisation and other sources — actual agronomic NUE accounting for all N inputs is typically lower.

question.question: Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for their development of CRISPR-Cas9. What was the key methodological contribution of their landmark 2012 *Science* paper?
options: They discovered the CRISPR loci in bacterial genomes — the original discovery was made by Yoshizumi Ishino (1987) and Francisco Mojica characterised CRISPR repeats in *Haloferax mediterranei* through the 1990s; Doudna and Charpentier's contribution was mechanistic and engineering, not the initial discovery.

They demonstrated that Cas9 could be programmed with a single guide RNA (sgRNA) to cleave double-stranded DNA at a specific target sequence defined by the guide sequence, showing the system could be repurposed as a programmable, precise genome-editing tool applicable to any organism. The 2012 *Science* paper (Jinek, Chylinski, Fonfara, Hauer, Doudna, Charpentier) reconstituted the *Streptococcus pyogenes* Cas9 system in vitro, showed that a dual-RNA guide (later simplified to a single chimeric sgRNA) directs Cas9 to cut DNA at a complementary target, and demonstrated cleavage at defined sites. This distinguished CRISPR-Cas9 from earlier programmable nucleases (ZFNs, TALENs) in its simplicity and versatility. The first demonstrations in human cells followed rapidly (Zhang lab at Broad; Church lab at Harvard, both published January 2013 in *Science*).

They developed the first plant transformation method for rice using CRISPR — plant CRISPR editing was first demonstrated by several groups simultaneously in 2013, not in the Doudna/Charpentier 2012 paper.
They invented the delivery system (AAV vector) used to introduce CRISPR into animal cells — AAV delivery is a separate biotechnology development not part of the 2012 paper.
question.explanation: The 2012 Jinek et al. *Science* paper showed Cas9 can be programmed with a single guide RNA to cut specific DNA sequences — a programmable molecular scissors applicable to any genome. This was the key insight enabling CRISPR as a general editing platform.

hints: Think about what makes CRISPR programmable — the guide molecule.
The 2012 paper was primarily in vitro biochemistry, not yet in cells.
slides.workedSolution: Doudna, Charpentier, and colleagues showed in 2012 that Cas9 is a programmable endonuclease guided to its target by a dual RNA (later simplified to sgRNA). Any 20-nucleotide guide sequence can be synthesised to direct Cas9 to any complementary DNA sequence — making genome editing as simple as ordering a short RNA. This programmability was the conceptual breakthrough; the Nobel Committee recognised it as enabling "a new tool for genome surgery."

question.question: Evaluate the carbon sequestration potential of converting a conventional corn field to a cover-cropped no-till system
question.goal: A 200 ha corn farm in Illinois currently under conventional till with no cover crops has soil organic carbon (SOC) at 2.1% in the top 30 cm. Soil bulk density is 1.3 t/m3. If switching to no-till + cereal rye cover crop increases SOC by 0.08% per year, calculate: (a) current SOC stock in t C/ha, (b) annual SOC gain in t C/ha/year under the new system, (c) carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) sequestered per hectare per year (molecular weight ratio CO2/C = 44/12).

steps.prompt: Calculate the current SOC stock (t C/ha) in the top 30 cm. SOC = 2.1% = 0.021 kg C per kg soil. Bulk density = 1.3 t/m3. Depth = 0.30 m.
steps.motivation: SOC stock = bulk density × depth × SOC fraction × unit conversion.
hints: Volume of top 30 cm per hectare = 1 ha × 0.30 m = 3,000 m3/ha. Mass of soil = 3,000 m3 × 1.3 t/m3 = 3,900 t/ha. SOC = 3,900 × 0.021.
steps.reveal: Volume = 10,000 m2 × 0.30 m = 3,000 m3/ha. Soil mass = 3,000 × 1.3 = 3,900 t/ha. SOC stock = 3,900 × 0.021 = 81.9 t C/ha. This is a standard soil carbon accounting calculation used by carbon markets and the IPCC.

steps.prompt: Calculate the annual SOC gain (t C/ha/year) from the 0.08% per year increase in SOC fraction. Use the same bulk density and depth.
steps.motivation: Translate a relative SOC change into an absolute sequestration rate.
hints: Annual SOC gain = 3,900 t soil/ha × 0.0008 (= 0.08% as a fraction).
steps.reveal: Annual SOC gain = 3,900 t soil/ha × 0.0008 = 3.12 t C/ha/year. This is consistent with published meta-analyses of no-till + cover crop systems: Poeplau and Don (2015) in *Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment* found cover crops increase SOC by 0.32 ± 0.08% per year on average across European trials.

steps.prompt: Convert the annual C gain to CO2e sequestered per hectare per year. Molecular weight of CO2 = 44 g/mol; C = 12 g/mol.
steps.motivation: Climate reporting requires CO2 equivalent units.
steps.reveal: CO2e = 3.12 × (44/12) = 3.12 × 3.667 = 11.44 t CO2e/ha/year. Over 200 ha, the farm sequesters approximately 2,288 t CO2e/year — equivalent to removing ~500 average US passenger vehicles from the road. This is the calculation basis for soil carbon credits in compliance markets (California cap-and-trade, EU ETS agricultural offsets).

question.prompt: In ≤180 words, explain what the planetary boundaries framework is, name three boundaries most transgressed by agriculture, and describe two specific regenerative or frontier practices (from cover crops, no-till, CRISPR, or vertical farming) that directly address at least one of those boundaries. Cite Rockström et al. (2009) in *Nature*, the 4 per 1000 Initiative, and either the EAT-Lancet Commission (2019) or Foley et al. (2011) in *Nature*.
question.rubric: Must define planetary boundaries as quantitative limits on Earth-system processes beyond which the risk of abrupt or irreversible change increases, citing Rockström et al. (2009). Must name at least three agriculture-driven boundaries: biogeochemical flows (N/P), land-system change, freshwater change, and/or biodiversity loss. Must describe two specific practices with mechanistic connection to a boundary — e.g., cover crops + no-till building SOC and reducing N leaching (biogeochemical boundary), or CRISPR-edited disease-resistant varieties reducing fungicide use and N fertiliser requirements. Should cite the 4 per 1000 Initiative (COP21, 2015, Le Foll) as a policy crystallisation of SOC sequestration. Bonus: cite EAT-Lancet (Willett et al. 2019) for diet-side demand management, or Foley et al. (2011) for the yield-gap/food-waste/diet-shift framework as an alternative to cropland expansion.
